transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
- Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dan Roman.
Democrats in January will have the largest house majority
since the 1990s.
This is after a race call Sunday for Democrats
by the AP in North Carolina.
NPR's Eric McDaniel reports.
- The Associated Press says Democrat Chuck Hubbard
has ousted Republican incumbent Virginia Fox.
He'll represent the northwest corner of the state
near Greensboro.
It's a notable win,
not just because Fox was an 83-year-old committee chair
who'd been in Washington more than 20 years,
but also because it puts the running tally
of Democratic House seats at 258,
matching the high watermark for either party
that stretches back to the 1992 election.
And there are still a handful of races left to call.
It could push their majority even higher.
Democrats also have a commanding Senate majority
that will need to work with President Trump
to get things signed into law, Eric McDaniel,
and PR News in Washington.
- Atlanta-based Delta Airline
says more than 1,000 flights were delayed Sunday
after an automated system used by flight crews
to calculate an aircraft's weight malfunction.
Sunday morning, the FAA issued a one-hour ground stop
at Delta's main hub at Atlanta-Hartsfield-Jackson
International Airport.
The FAA said the delays were not related
to the recent grounding of tens of thousands of flights
because of a computer malfunction.
Boston-based passenger Genevieve Tofasken
said she was concerned while waiting for her delayed flight.
- Technology just keeps having an issue.
It's so demoralizing.
It's very concerning and scary,
and I'm just really hoping that we get out today.
Want to get home for Thanksgiving.
- Before a flight, pilots and others calculate
the weight and balance on board the aircraft
to make sure it is within specifications.
The death of the beloved Hippo Fiona
after she swallowed a knit hat
is renewing calls to remind zoo visitors
that animals can die from swallowing foreign objects.
NPR's Shonda Lee-Stuster reports.
- While deaths like Fiona the Hippos are rare,
items such as coins, shoes, and sunglasses frequently fall
and sometimes are tossed into animal habitats at zoos.
Dr. Gabrielle Aflaca, a veterinarian at Zoo Miami,
asks that visitors follow zoo etiquette
and not yell or throw objects at the animals.
- If we can just keep in mind that anything that we bring
that could inadvertently end up in the animal exhibit
or somehow around the animal, try to just be mindful
and not have your sunglasses on your head
if you're leaning over and looking at something.
- Veterinarians say people should also be mindful of items
that can harm animals in the wild or even pets at home.
Human medication should be stored properly
and trash should be thrown into a garbage can
so animals cannot eat it.
Shonda Lee-Stuster, NPR News.
- It'll be a short week on Wall Street
because of the holiday markets close Thursday,
a half day on Friday.
It's NPR.
Researchers are developing brain implants
that can help restore people's speech and movement.
NPR's Ping Wang reports these technologies
can even help people sing.
- A 58-year-old train singer had lost much of her ability
to speak and sing due to ALS,
a disease that destroys nerve cells
that control muscle movement.
Maitreyi Wairakar is a neuroscientist at UC Davis.
She and her colleagues designed an implant
that connects to parts of the singer's brain
related to speech, pitch, and tone.
- We designed a task to enable her to sing a musical scale.
We asked her to sing a typical major scale
and we were able to decode all the notes
that she sang with very high accuracy.
♪ Ah, ah, ah ♪
- The implant records her brain signals into a computer
which translates them into commands.
The technology is still largely experimental
and was presented at the Society for Neuroscience Conference.
Ping Wang, NPR News.
- A New Orleans federal appeals court
by a vote of nine to eight has struck down a law
requiring accommodations for pregnant women
declaring it unconstitutional.
The court said the 2020 law was not valid
when it was passed by Congress
because it was approved by lawmakers
without a majority of the House members present.
At the time, Congress was operating
under the COVID era rules,
allowing members to vote by proxy.
The decision will impact women in Texas, Louisiana,
and Mississippi covered by the fifth U.S. Circuit.
Advocates for the law say they expect it will be going
eventually to the Supreme Court.
I'm Dan Ronan.
Support free.

topics.text: Democrat Chuck Hubbard ousts Republican Virginia Fox in North Carolina, giving Democrats 258 House seats
Delta Airlines delays over 1,000 flights after weight-calculation system malfunctions at Atlanta hub
Zoo veterinarians urge visitors to avoid throwing objects after hippo Fiona dies from swallowing a hat
Researchers develop brain implants that restore speech and singing ability for ALS patient
New Orleans federal appeals court strikes down pregnancy accommodations law over proxy voting in Congress
